{"id": "74:24/q01", "question": "Who uttered this judgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q01/p1", "position": "Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, the Quraysh leader called al-Wāḥid.", "reasons": "Jishumī, citing Ibn ʿĀmir, names him al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī, describes his wealth and sons, and says his people called him al-Wāḥid; Ibn Kathīr also identifies him as a Quraysh leader. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk links him to the solitary man of 74:11."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q02", "question": "What does the fāʾ in fa-qāla convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q02/p1", "position": "He voiced the accusation immediately after it occurred to him or after turning away in pride.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, al-Nasafī, and al-Ālūsī say the phrase was uttered without hesitation once conceived; al-Rāzī places it just after his proud turning away. Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the linked acts: frowning and scowling are close, pride causes turning away, and the fāʾ marks immediate utterance. Al-Bayḍāwī combines the inherited-magic gloss with this temporal point. Al-Ālūsī says immediacy does not conflict with the preceding report; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī traces the sequence from deliberation and looking through frowning, disgust, turning away, and pride."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q03", "question": "What is the force of in hādhā illā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q03/p1", "position": "It restricts his verdict to magic, presenting it as the outcome of rejecting other descriptions.", "reasons": "Bursevī says in is the negative particle mā, as the following illā shows. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the exclusive wording presents magic as the conclusion of his testing and sorting through possible descriptions, following 74:18."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q04", "question": "What does hādhā point to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q04/p1", "position": "The Qur’an, Muhammad’s recitation or message.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī explicitly identifies the demonstrative as the Qur’an; Bursevī does the same. Other accounts call its immediate object what Muhammad recited or his message."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q05", "question": "What does siḥr mean in this accusation?", "turns_on": "Whether siḥr is explained as deceptive sorcery or as the spellbinding effect of eloquence.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q05/p1", "position": "Sorcery or deception: an illusory effect presented as truth.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī glosses it as deception and reports a definition of magic as making falsehood appear true. Al-Biqāʿī says the accusation treats the message as effects without reality, with hidden causes. Asad gives the ordinary sense sorcery or magic and, citing Tāj al-ʿArūs, the primary sense of changing a thing from its natural state; when applied to revelation, it implies deliberate deception or delusion."}, {"id": "74:24/q05/p2", "position": "Something with the captivating effect of magic, especially exceptional eloquence.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says its sweetness affects souls as magic does. Abū Ḥayyān glosses illā siḥr as something resembling sorcery. Asad explains the figurative use for spellbinding eloquence and reads the charge as old spellbinding eloquence. Iṣlāḥī describes the leader’s misreading of stirring eloquence and says Quraysh adopted the label after they could no longer deny the Qur’an’s eloquence and force."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q06", "question": "What does yuʾthar mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether yuʾthar comes from recounting and transmitting earlier material or from īthār, preferring one thing over another.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q06/p1", "position": "It is transmitted, narrated, or learned from others before Muhammad.", "reasons": "Abū Razīn says the supposed magic was taken from someone else, in al-Ṭabarī and al-Durr. Al-Wāḥidī derives athara al-ḥadīth from following a people’s traces after death, later general narration, and cites ʿUmar’s wording about recalling or reporting an oath. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī give the reporting sense; al-Qurṭubī calls athara a verbal noun and maʾthūr a report from earlier generations, citing verses of Imruʾ al-Qays for what keeps being recounted and al-Aʿshā for al-athīr as hearer or transmitter. Abū Ḥayyān cites poetry for this sense. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī and Bursevī explain the transfer from another, with Bursevī distinguishing learning from performing magic. Bursevī also describes the old-to-general development of the verb. Al-Ālūsī prefers the retold, learned sense and invokes Babylonian magic; Elmalılı says practitioners teach it to successors. Al-Bayḍāwī allows both transmitted and learned."}, {"id": "74:24/q06/p2", "position": "It is chosen, preferred, or admired over other magic.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās derives it from īthār, preferring one thing, and says the Qur’an would be preferred above magic. Al-Rāzī gives the same alternative; Abū Ḥayyān reports it alongside transmission; Elmalılı describes a dazzling, captivating appeal. Al-Ṭabrisī reports that souls favor and choose it because of sweetness. Al-Ālūsī mentions but does not select this interpretation."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q07", "question": "From whom did he allege that the magic was learned?", "turns_on": "The reports name a general earlier source, Musaylima, Babylon, or both; Abū Ḥayyān explicitly gives Musaylima or Babylon.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q07/p1", "position": "From earlier people or sorcerers, left unnamed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says another person; al-Māwardī's Ibn Zayd says earlier people; al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nasafī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī say sorcerers. Al-Wāḥidī al-Wajīz likewise says sorcerers; al-Biqāʿī adds that a listener passes it to another and that the alleged magic divides spouses and close relatives. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the alleged sources as ancient people."}, {"id": "74:24/q07/p2", "position": "From Musaylima.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī explicitly names Musaylima; al-Farrāʾ, al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī give him alongside Babylonian sorcerers. Abū Ḥayyān’s debate report gives Musaylima or Babylon as alternatives."}, {"id": "74:24/q07/p3", "position": "From Babylonian sorcerers or the people of Babylon.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī names the people of Babylon; al-Farrāʾ names Babylonian sorcerers and separately says Muhammad learned it from them. Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī pair Babylon with Musaylima; Abū Ḥayyān reports Babylon as an alternative, and al-Ālūsī refers to Babylon and similar sources."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q08", "question": "Why call the supposed magic inherited?", "turns_on": "Whether the qualifier chiefly answers an objection from the message’s unusual character or explains away its captivating effect as inherited human speech.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q08/p1", "position": "To explain why the Qur’an and Muhammad did not resemble familiar magic or magicians.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says he posited unfamiliar magical sayings from ancient people to account for the Qur’an’s distinct language and effects and for Muhammad’s circumstances."}, {"id": "74:24/q08/p2", "position": "To present its powerful effect as familiar human artistry passed down from earlier speakers.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says opponents conceded its spellbinding effect but attributed it to earlier poets and orators, denying that it was divine or unique. Al-Biqāʿī notes the alleged magic spreads powerfully and divides families."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q09", "question": "What happened before al-Walīd made this accusation?", "turns_on": "The narratives differ over Abū Jahl’s intervention, a Quraysh council, individual encounters with recitation, and the Fuṣṣilat episode.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q09/p1", "position": "He praised the Qur’an, then Abū Jahl pressured him to denounce it.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr says the recitation softened him, he praised its sweetness and force, and Abū Jahl pressed him. Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr says he initially called it God’s speech, neither poetry, magic nor madness, and Abū Jahl shamed him by fearing conversion. Al-Wāḥidī and Study Quran report praise of its unlike-poetry, sweet and abundant language. Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī also record rejecting madness, soothsaying, poetry and lying before the verdict, with Musaylima and Babylon named. Abū Ḥayyān’s second report says visits to Abū Bakr and Quraysh’s suspicions formed Abū Jahl’s pressure. Elmalılı adds the charge that al-Walīd had strayed, his wealth and poetry expertise, public denunciation, the assembly’s applause and dispersal; his praise included beauty, fruitfulness and incomparable height. Ibn Isḥāq and other historians in Ibn Kathīr report a similar account."}, {"id": "74:24/q09/p2", "position": "A Quraysh discussion of possible labels led him to choose magic after rejecting the others.", "reasons": "Mujāhid in al-Wāḥidī gives madman, soothsayer, poet, and liar as rejected labels. Jishumī says al-Walīd chose magician because the Qur’an divided families. Ibn Kathīr’s al-Suddī places a council before the pilgrimage to deter visitors. Al-Durr’s Mujāhid from Ibn ʿAbbās credits al-Walīd’s poetry and soothsaying expertise for rejecting those labels. Abū Ḥayyān reports variants of a debate with Abū Jahl and Quraysh with the same gist, including praise of sweetness and force. Al-Wāḥidī records Quraysh asking for his verdict; Study Quran notes he settled on sorcery after considering alternatives."}, {"id": "74:24/q09/p3", "position": "He heard or examined recitation, deliberated, then pronounced it magic.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd in al-Ṭabarī says he watched Muhammad reciting in prayer, found the words sweet and heart-gripping, rejected poetry and soothsaying, then allowed inherited magic. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says Muhammad invited him to Islam and he delayed, pondered, frowned and turned away before the verdict and Saqar. Qatāda in al-Durr reports praise of sweetness, beauty, fruitfulness and dominance despite the magic verdict. Al-Farrāʾ locates a scene near Muslims at the Sacred Mosque, where he ca

lled Muhammad a sorcerer, then scowled and turned away."}, {"id": "74:24/q09/p4", "position": "A reported encounter with the opening of Fuṣṣilat preceded his rejection.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān connects the rejection with his hearing Muhammad recite the opening of Fuṣṣilat and pleading for him to stop at the warning about ʿĀd and Thamūd, 41:13."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q10", "question": "Which verses did the reported incident occasion?", "turns_on": "Whether the incident belongs to the opening passages of both sūras or specifically to these verses; Elmalılı cites the recited Ḥā-Mīm passages.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q10/p1", "position": "The account concerns the opening of al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports that some attach the incident to the beginnings of both sūras."}, {"id": "74:24/q10/p2", "position": "It concerns these al-Muddaththir verses, including 74:11–24.", "reasons": "Elmalılı argues for these verses because the passages recited were from the Ḥā-Mīms. Al-Ṭabarī’s ʿIkrima and Ibn ʿAbbās reports say the passage was revealed after the charge; al-Wāḥidī specifies 74:11–24. Qatāda in al-Durr says the condemnation from his measuring through becoming sullen was revealed about him; Study Quran’s Ibn ʿAbbās account likewise says the verdict prompted this passage."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q11", "question": "What accusation about the Qur’an does the verse express?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusation is explained as inherited sorcery or as a disparaging account of the Qur’an’s captivating eloquence.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q11/p1", "position": "He alleges that the Qur’an is humanly transmitted magic, rather than divine revelation.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn Kathīr, Bursevī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Elmalılı pair this charge with calling it human speech, where stated. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says exegetes understand the claim as falsely presented revelation; al-Wāḥidī says Muhammad took it from Musaylima. Al-Biqāʿī says the alleged effects lack reality and points out Muhammad neither practiced nor learned magic. Iṣlāḥī says opponents used the label as propaganda after its force could no longer be denied."}, {"id": "74:24/q11/p2", "position": "He treats the Qur’an as captivating human eloquence or influence, comparing it with magic.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes its effect to sweetness; Asad reads old spellbinding eloquence. Iṣlāḥī says he misjudged the prophet’s stirring eloquence and that opponents compared its effect with earlier poets and orators; Abū Ḥayyān explains the magic phrase as resemblance."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q12", "question": "What does his verdict reveal about his response to revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the note emphasizes his own conscious rejection or extends the portrayal to similarly dismissive readers.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q12/p1", "position": "He knowingly or pridefully rejected the truth and fashioned a false excuse.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Bursevī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī connect the speech with arrogant turning away. Al-Naḥḥās says he found no argument, disbelieved, then made the claim. Al-Burhān says pride made him recant recognition. Al-Biqāʿī says corrupt worldly calculation ignored God’s judgment and the Hereafter, and that Muhammad’s lack of magical practice or learning exposes the charge. Iṣlāḥī calls it a disdainfully delivered excuse ignoring a warning whose realities he will meet. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates worldly leadership and envy to a worldly threat and denial of revelation to the threat of Hell. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s account ends with Saqar."}, {"id": "74:24/q12/p2", "position": "The condemnation also applies to others who adopt the same unbelieving posture.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu reads 74:18–25 as condemning people like al-Walīd, not only the individual in the report."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q13", "question": "How is this verdict connected with neighboring verses and other Qur’anic charges?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the verdict either to its immediate continuation and punishment or to parallel Qur’anic accusations.", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q13/p1", "position": "The following human-speech accusation confirms this one, and the threats answer his worldly motives and denial.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says the second accusation is unjoined because it confirms the first. Ibn ʿĀshūr says worldly threat answers his pursuit of leadership and envy, while Hell answers his attack on the Qur’an and denial of revelation, citing 74:14 and 74:24–26."}, {"id": "74:24/q13/p2", "position": "Other Qur’anic passages portray similar fabricated labels and the deniers’ failure.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says the Qur’an elsewhere describes the disbelievers inventing comparisons and losing the way. Study Quran cites other opponents calling revelations manifest sorcery at 5:110, 6:7, 11:7, 34:43 and 37:15."}]}
{"id": "74:24/q14", "question": "What ruling about learning and practicing magic is drawn here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:24/q14/p1", "position": "Learning it for a sound purpose is allowed, but believing in its reality and practicing it are disbelief.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites a couplet saying knowledge of evil can protect a person from it."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q01", "question": "What does تُبْقِى mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q01/p1", "position": "To spare, preserve, or leave something remaining; it can also suggest prolonging life or showing compassion.", "reasons": "Jishumi defines ibqāʾ as leaving some of what was taken, cites abqāhu Allāh for God prolonging a life, and explains al-bāqī as what continues to exist. Bursevi's Persian glossary gives preservation and compassion."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q02", "question": "How is the form تذر explained?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q02/p1", "position": "Its initial wāw is dropped by analogy with يذر, a verb without a past form and equivalent in meaning to يدع.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysān supplies the analogy, as reported by Nahhas."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q03", "question": "How is the final rāʾ of تذر pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q03/p1", "position": "When made sākin after a fatḥa, its rāʾ is emphatic for all readers.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari uses ولا تذر as the example. He contrasts a final sākin rāʾ after kasra, which stays light even before an emphatic letter because the letter is separated from the rāʾ."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q04", "question": "How is the clause attached grammatically to the description of Saqar?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is predication or explanation, an independent statement, or a ḥāl governed by the preceding rhetorical question; Al-Alusi disputes the last analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q04/p1", "position": "It describes or explains Saqar, including analysis as another predicate of Saqar.", "reasons": "Baydawi allows an explanation of Saqar's nature or a circumstantial description. Al-Alusi calls it explanatory; Ibn Ashur says it elaborates the terror of the preceding question and serves as another predicate. Ibn Ashur says the coordinated ولا تذر has circumstantial force."}, {"id": "74:28/q04/p2", "position": "It is an independent sentence.", "reasons": "Samin reports this as a second syntactic analysis; Al-Alusi also allows an independent explanatory clause and says no omitted subject need be posited."}, {"id": "74:28/q04/p3", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause governed by the sense of magnification in the preceding question about Saqar.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa gives this analysis in Samin. Baydawi also permits a circumstantial description. Al-Alusi reports the analysis but finds it unconvincing."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q05", "question": "What does Saqar leave or spare?", "turns_on": "What the unstated object and scope of the two negated verbs are: everything thrown in, every person, every body part, every form of torment, or relief from torment.", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q05/p1", "position": "Nothing cast into Saqar escapes its consuming destruction.", "reasons": "Thalabi says it destroys whatever enters. Abu Muslim calls this the ultimate description of burning. Kashshaf and Al-Alusi stress inevitable destruction of all that is thrown in; Baydawi says it neither leaves anything nor spares it before destroying it. Samin supplies the omitted object, what is cast in. Nasafi allows that nothing remains intact. Biqai extends this to every condition, distinguishing destruction from alteration of those punished. Kuranyolu connects the verse to burning and scorched skin; Bursevi cites 4:56 for renewed burning."}, {"id": "74:28/q05/p2", "position": "No part of its victims' bodies remains unburned, especially flesh, bone, blood, skin, sinew, veins, or marrow.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi specifies flesh and bone in Thalabi, Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Qurtubi, and Al-Alusi. Qurtubi and the Ibn Abbas report through Ata add blood; the latter says renewed burning becomes more intense. Ibn Burayda and Abu Sinan name flesh, veins, nerves, skin, sinew, and marrow. Nasafi and Al-Alusi divide flesh and bone between the two verbs; Al-Alusi calls that explanation weaker. Ibn Ashur says the omitted object can include every body part. Study Quran reports the bones, skin, and blood interpretation."}, {"id": "74:28/q05/p3", "position": "No person deserving Saqar's punishment escapes being seized or tormented.", "reasons": "Ibn Isa says none is spared seizure or punishment; Jishumi reports that everyone in Hell is reached. Razi distinguishes the first verb as covering every deserving person and the second as covering every body part. Samin and Ibn Ashur give a person cast in, or no one at all, as the omitted object. Abu Hayyan says no one thrown in remains untouched."}, {"id": "74:28/q05/p4", "position": "Saqar withholds no type, degree, or full force of torment.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says it leaves no kind or limit of torment untouched. Al-Jubba'i and Abu Ali say it burns

 all and spares none of the full range of torments; Abu Ali adds that the victims are exhausted. Abu Hayyan says it delivers every degree. Samin suggests any degree of torment as the omitted object. Razi distinguishes exhaustive bodily burning from using all the fire's power and intensity."}, {"id": "74:28/q05/p5", "position": "It grants no mercy, health, relief, or respite, and does not release its victim.", "reasons": "Mawardi's further possibility denies health and respite. Bursevi's alternative denies mercy, supported by his Persian gloss of ibqāʾ as preservation or compassion. Elmalili says the victim is never released; Islahi says Hell neither eases agony nor spares anyone and remains vigilant. Muqatil says it overtakes them even when they swear."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q06", "question": "What happens to the victims after Saqar consumes them?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes describe the cycle of destruction and recreation or its resulting state of neither life nor death; several sources combine both.", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q06/p1", "position": "They are recreated or given new skin or bodies, and Saqar burns them again without end.", "reasons": "Marthad, Muqatil, Al-Dahhak, Al-Kalbi, Ibn Abbas, and others describe renewed seizing after recreation; Muqatil and Ibn Abbas mention changed skins or bodies. Ata from Ibn Abbas describes burning to charcoal and a more severe renewed punishment; Razi's Ibn Abbas report adds blood, flesh, and bone and repeated intensification. Al-Dahhak also says Hell never tires. Kashshaf and Al-Alusi explicitly distinguish destruction from leaving them dead; Bursevi and Ibn Ashur cite 4:56, and Study Quran cites 87:12-13 and 4:56. Elmalili stresses that Saqar does not release them."}, {"id": "74:28/q06/p2", "position": "The Fire neither lets its inhabitants live nor lets them die.", "reasons": "Mujahid is reported by Tabari, Thalabi, Mawardi, Jishumi, Baghawi, and Qurtubi; several of these explain that burning resumes after recreation. Tabari states that they are destroyed and renewed; Ibn Burayda and Abu Sinan associate the state with consumed and replaced bodily tissue. Asad and Study Quran also give this reading; Study Quran cites 87:12-13 and 4:56."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q07", "question": "What do the two near-parallel negations contribute rhetorically?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair is emphatic synonymy, cumulative wording, or a division between persons, body parts, the intensity of torment, and successive destruction and restoration.", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q07/p1", "position": "They repeat near-synonymous senses for emphasis and complete negation.", "reasons": "Razi compares paired synonyms to saying someone turned away and avoided him. Qurtubi calls the repetition an emphasis of total bodily burning. Suyuti lists coordinated near-synonyms as a rhetorical type. Al-Mubarrad disputes the existence of such Qur'anic synonym pairs, so his note argues against this analysis."}, {"id": "74:28/q07/p2", "position": "The paired terms together add meaning beyond either verb alone.", "reasons": "An unnamed view in Itqan compares added meaning from paired terms to meaning added by extra letters. Suyuti warns against alleging needless repetition and cites this phrase alongside 2:157. Al-Zarkashi says discourse structure, including metaphor, adds meaning and should stop an exegete from assuming simple synonymy. Al-Mubarrad also insists the paired words have distinct senses."}, {"id": "74:28/q07/p3", "position": "The first verb describes consuming or destroying; the second describes renewed punishment rather than leaving victims dead or alone.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Al-Alusi explicitly distinguish destruction and restoration. Ibn Jawzi and reports from Muqatil, Al-Kalbi, Ibn Abbas, Al-Dahhak, and others divide consumption from pursuit after recreated skin or bodies; Bursevi and Ibn Ashur use 4:56 for renewal."}, {"id": "74:28/q07/p4", "position": "The first leaves no deserving person untormented; the second leaves no part of their bodies unburned.", "reasons": "Razi reports this as one distinction made by others."}, {"id": "74:28/q07/p5", "position": "The first leaves no body part; the second applies the Fire's full power and intensity.", "reasons": "Razi reports this as a further distinction."}, {"id": "74:28/q07/p6", "position": "The first consumes flesh; the second spares no bone.", "reasons": "Nasafi gives this division, and Al-Alusi reports it from Al-Suddi but ranks it weaker than the preceding explanations."}, {"id": "74:28/q07/p7", "position": "The pair excludes both anything remaining unharmed and anything escaping destruction.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Al-Alusi frame this as nothing spared and nothing released from destruction; Baydawi likewise says nothing is left before being destroyed."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q08", "question": "Does Saqar tire or give its victims respite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q08/p1", "position": "It never tires or weakens and allows no pause, relief, or respite from punishment.", "reasons": "Thalabi says everything has a pause and weariness except Hell. Al-Dahhak says the same in Jishumi and Baghawi, and Al-Alusi repeats that everything else slackens. Biqai says Saqar destroys or alters without fatigue; Mawardi denies respite, and Islahi says it remains wholly vigilant without easing agony."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q09", "question": "How does this description work as a warning in its passage?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either the warning's general audience or the different responses to its terrifying presentation.", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q09/p1", "position": "It warns humankind generally by portraying Saqar's terrifying destruction.", "reasons": "Farra says the description warns humankind and explains nadhīr as warning, citing analogous language at 54:16 and 67:18. Islahi says the general warning is not addressed to Muhammad and Hell's horror exceeds worldly imagination. Kuranyolu says verses 27–28 portray a terrifying place that spares nothing and scorches human skin."}, {"id": "74:28/q09/p2", "position": "Its astonishing scale exposes the folly of arrogant disbelief and benefits seekers of truth.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says the preceding question expresses amazement at Saqar's enormity. Ibn Ashur says the clause elaborates the terror of that question. Islahi says disbelievers mock Hell from imagined omniscience, whereas the warning rests on divine wisdom: truth seekers benefit and arrogant people ruin their fate."}]}
{"id": "74:28/q10", "question": "How should this portrayal of the hereafter be understood?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:28/q10/p1", "position": "Allegorically, as part of the Qur'an's descriptions of the hereafter.", "reasons": "Asad says the following verse and verses 28 onward indicate this reading."}]}

{"id": "74:35/q11", "question": "What do the two readings of the preceding night-oath say?", "turns_on": "The time adverb and verb form for the night’s departure; Ibn Ashur regards both as sound.", "positions": [{"id": "74:35/q11/p1", "position": "إذ أدبر uses إذ with a past-tense form, swearing by the recurring moment when night has departed.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur attributes it to Nafi, Hamza, Hafs, Yaqub and Khalaf."}, {"id": "74:35/q11/p2", "position": "إذا دبر uses the future-time adverb and a plain verb meaning departed, parallel to إذا أسفر.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur attributes it to Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr, Abu Bakr from Asim, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far; he says both readings are sound."}]}
{"id": "74:35/q12", "question": "How do inward readings understand the great warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the spiritual danger is renewed injustice and darkness, unreflective conformity, or descent into nature and bodily desire.", "positions": [{"id": "74:35/q12/p1", "position": "It warns against a return to injustice or inward darkness after illumination.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami says warning to humanity confirms the matter for those granted direct illumination; al-Qushayri fears darkness returning to hearts after reality is disclosed."}, {"id": "74:35/q12/p2", "position": "Prophetic warning returns those absorbed in conformity to spiritual witnessing, though conformity has no significance at direct vision.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports al-Wasiti: lights appear to the spirits of the unifiers, and warning calls them back to their witness."}, {"id": "74:35/q12/p3", "position": "Saqar signifies nature or the lower self's hell; its warning benefits receptive souls who can rise toward heart and spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani contrasts receptive people who attain virtues with others descending into bodily desire. {"id": "74:35/q13", "question": "What other rhetorical effects are noted around this verse?", "turns_on": "The notes identify separate rhetorical devices in the surrounding discussion: emphasis, paronomasia, and added nuance from arrangement.", "positions": [{"id": "74:35/q13/p1", "position": "Repetition lends emphasis.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda illustrates this with repeated 'I saw,' awlā laka, three plus seven restated as ten, and the reiterated curse of Abu Lahab."}, {"id": "74:35/q13/p2", "position": "The two occurrences of البشر form complete paronomasia.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares the occurrence in the passage with لواحة للبشر at 74:29."}, {"id": "74:35/q13/p3", "position": "Rhetorical merit comes from a phrase's arrangement and the extra nuance it conveys.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani compares كأن زيدا الأسد with زيد كالأسد: the former makes Zayd's bravery seem indistinguishable from a lion's."}]}

{"id": "74:42/q10", "question": "How is the sinners' answer about what brought them to Saqar explained?", "turns_on": "The positions explain different parts of the reply rather than dispute a single reading; al-Rāzī specifies legal obligations, while Ibn Kathīr states the broader religious and social failures.", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q10/p1", "position": "Their failure to pray and feed the poor means omission of obligatory prayer and zakat.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reasons that punishment cannot attach to omitting merely voluntary acts."}, {"id": "74:42/q10/p2", "position": "Their failure to pray and feed the poor means they neither worshipped God nor did good to people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr sets the two omissions alongside duties to God and fellow humans."}, {"id": "74:42/q10/p3", "position": "Joining those who delved means engaging in falsehood.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī explains the third confession this way."}, {"id": "74:42/q10/p4", "position": "The coming of 'certainty' means death, until which they denied resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 15:99 for the sense of certainty as death."}]}
{"id": "74:42/q11", "question": "Does the reply assign all four confessed faults to each condemned person?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q11/p1", "position": "Its apparent wording assigns all four faults to each member of the condemned groups.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī explicitly draws this inference from the wording."}]}
{"id": "74:42/q12", "question": "Why is denial of judgment placed last among the offenses?", "turns_on": "Whether the ordering chiefly stresses persistence in denial or a progression from neglected practices to disbelief.", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q12/p1", "position": "Its last place stresses that the criminals persisted in this worst fault after the preceding three.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls denial of judgment the worst fault and cites 90:17."}, {"id": "74:42/q12/p2", "position": "The sequence moves from lack of Muslim practice to the graver sin of disbelief and denial of Judgment.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān compares the progression with 90:11 and 90:17."}]}
{"id": "74:42/q13", "question": "Are unbelievers punished for neglecting subsidiary religious duties?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q13/p1", "position": "Yes; the verse supports their punishment for omitting subsidiary rules of religious law.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports his school's argument and refers detailed treatment to al-Maḥṣūl; his interpretation of prayer and feeding as obligations supports it."}]}
{"id": "74:42/q14", "question": "What does the passage teach about whose deeds can save or condemn a soul?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q14/p1", "position": "Each soul is held for its own deeds; no other's deeds or intercession free it or avert its Hell.", "reasons": "Islahi draws this from the passage's contrast between the people of the right and those held for their crimes."}]}
{"id": "74:42/q15", "question": "How does this exchange serve the sura's warning about the Hereafter?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q15/p1", "position": "The Qurʾān warns people to prepare for the Hereafter; evaders have only stubbornness as an excuse.", "reasons": "Islahi says manifestations of nature argue for the Hereafter and expose heedlessness, while the warning gives people a chance to prepare."}]}
{"id": "74:42/q16", "question": "What does Anas's report say about the condemned person's lost chance to avoid Hell?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:42/q16/p1", "position": "The lowest-ranking person in Hell would ransom himself with the earth's weight in gold, though he had failed to ask God for much easier help and forgiveness.", "reasons": "In Anas's prophetic report, God recalls those earlier requests that the person never made or feared; the report says no one is worse than him and relates to 74:42–48."}]}
{"id": "74:49/q01", "question": "How does the preceding passage set up this rebuke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:49/q01/p1", "position": "The prior account supplies reasons to heed the reminder, making their continued rejection astonishing and baseless.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya points to the judgment and intercession just described; Abū Ḥayyān says they turn away while awaiting that situation. Bursawī points to the dreadful fate and ample reasons to heed the Qur'an. Ālūsī says the fāʾ orders the rebuke after reasons to accept and reflect. Ibn ʿĀshūr links it to the Qur'an's description as a reminder for humankind in 74:31. Ṭabāṭabāʾī points to the preceding threat and promise and says they seek individual revelation despite manifest truth. Iṣlāḥī mentions advance warning, a revealed Book, and a messenger."}]}
{"id": "74:49/q02", "question": "What force does the question فما لهم have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:49/q02/p1", "position": "It rebukes and expresses amazement that they turn away without good cause despite what they have received.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says mā shaʾnuka/mā laka carries the sense 'why?' Al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz asks why they reject the Prophet's admonition; Ṭabrisī asks why they reject the Qur'an's admonitions. Qurṭubī frames it as why Mecca's people turn from the brought message.
